planting.note: Divide established clumps in early spring or fall and set crowns just below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil under deciduous cover; fresh seed has deep double dormancy and can take 18–24 months to germinate even with cold-moist stratification, so division is the practical propagation method.

directions: Divide established clumps in early spring or fall and set crowns just below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich woodland soil under deciduous cover. This European relative of American baneberries and black cohosh produces feathery compound foliage and small white bottlebrush flower spikes in late spring, followed by glossy black berries that are showy but toxic if eaten, so it is grown strictly as an ornamental or wildlife plant rather than an edible. It prefers cool, shaded, humusy sites such as beech or hazel woodland and resents drying out during summer. Established plants are long-lived and slowly clump-forming rather than aggressive spreaders.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil; this hybrid mayapple establishes and spreads more slowly than the native species, so be patient and avoid frequent disturbance.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil and be patient, since this hybrid mayapple establishes and spreads slowly compared to the native species. It is grown chiefly for its spectacular umbrella-shaped leaves, which emerge deep chocolate-mahogany with irregular jade-green mottling before shifting to a more solid bronze-green as the season progresses. Small nodding flowers appear beneath the foliage canopy in spring, but the plant is prized almost entirely for its foliage display in a shaded border or container. Mulch to keep roots cool and protect emerging shoots from late frost.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers in fall, several inches deep, in humus-rich soil beneath deciduous trees or shrubs where the plant will get bright spring light before the canopy leafs out.

directions: Plant dormant tubers in fall, several inches deep, in humus-rich soil beneath deciduous trees or shrubs where the plant will get bright spring light before the canopy leafs out. This close cousin of the more common Corydalis solida is a true spring ephemeral, pushing up ferny gray-green foliage and dense spikes of purple, pink, or occasionally white flowers in earliest spring before vanishing completely by early summer. Its hollow, chambered tuber distinguishes it from solid-tubered relatives, and it slowly naturalizes into loose colonies in cool woodland gardens. Avoid disturbing the site in summer since the plant is dormant and invisible underground.

planting.note: Divide the slender creeping rhizomes in fall and plant shallowly in loose, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees where the colony can receive bright early-spring light; seed germination is slow and erratic, so division is the practical propagation method.

directions: Divide the slender creeping rhizomes in fall and plant shallowly in loose, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees where the colony can receive bright early-spring light. Native to eastern North American woodlands, this dainty spring ephemeral bears five-parted leaflets and solitary white, often pink-blushed flowers that open in mid to late spring, then the whole plant goes dormant and disappears by midsummer as the canopy closes overhead. It differs from the similar European wood anemone in leaflet number and is a well-behaved, slow-spreading groundcover rather than an aggressive colonizer. Best combined with other spring ephemerals like trout lily or spring beauty that share the same fleeting bloom window.

common_name: Chocolate Ruffles Heuchera (Chocolate Ruffles Coral Bells)

planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-amended soil in partial shade, since strong afternoon sun can scorch its large leaves.

directions: Set divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-amended soil in partial shade, since strong afternoon sun can scorch its large leaves. This heavily ruffled Heuchera villosa-type hybrid produces broad, deeply savoyed foliage in rich milk-chocolate brown, held above the soil in a loose mound, with airy white flower spikes rising well above the leaves in summer. Its villosa parentage gives it noticeably better heat and humidity tolerance than many glossier heuchera hybrids, making it a good performer in warm-summer regions like the Gulf South. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep the crown vigorous.
